screening.reason: Inclusion 2/3: analyses ABIDE resting-state functional connectivity explicitly and reports a diagnostic classification analysis (autism vs. typical development).

evidence_spans.text: We attempted to replicate the method and results using the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) including resting state fMRI data obtained from 964 subjects and 16 separate international sites.
evidence_spans.claim: Study replicates a single-site connectivity classification approach on a 964-subject, 16-site ABIDE sample.

evidence_spans.text: A total of 964 subjects met all inclusion criteria (517 typically developing subjects and 447 subjects with autism from 16 sites).
evidence_spans.claim: Analysed cohort: 964 ABIDE I participants (447 autism, 517 typically developing) from 16 sites after applying inclusion criteria.

evidence_spans.text: Inclusion criteria for subjects were successful preprocessing with manual visual inspection of normalization to MNI space of MPRAGE, coregistration of BOLD and MPRAGE images, seg- mentation of MPRAG
evidence_spans.claim: QC rule was manual visual inspection of normalization/coregistration/segmentation success, not a numeric motion threshold at the subject-inclusion stage.

evidence_spans.text: Motion scrubbing (Power et al., 2012) of framewise dis- placement and DVARS with removal of volumes before and after a root-mean-square displace
evidence_spans.claim: Motion was handled via framewise-displacement/DVARS-based scrubbing of individual volumes.

evidence_spans.text: Overall, a leave-one-out classiﬁer was used to generate a classiﬁcation score for each of the 964 subjects, leaving out one subject at a time and calculating the classiﬁcation score for the left out sub- ject.
evidence_spans.claim: Evaluation used a leave-one-subject-out classifier across all 964 subjects.

evidence_spans.text: Age, age-squared, gender, handedness, and site were included as covariates for the classiﬁer.
evidence_spans.claim: Site was included as a covariate adjusted for in the classifier.

evidence_spans.text: As high as 60% accuracy was obtained for whole brain classiﬁcation, with the best accuracy from connections involving regions of the default mode network, parahippocampaland fusiform gyri, insula, Wernicke Area, and intraparietal sulcus.
evidence_spans.claim: Best whole-brain classification accuracy was 60%, driven by default-mode, parahippocampal/fusiform, insula, Wernicke and intraparietal-sulcus connections.

evidence_spans.text: Multisite functional connectivity classiﬁcation of autism outperformed chance using a simple leave-one-out classiﬁer, but exhibited poorer accuracy than for single site results.
evidence_spans.claim: Multisite classification outperformed chance but underperformed prior single-site classification results.

assessments.support: 964 of 1112 ABIDE I subjects (447 autism/517 TD) from 16 sites retained after explicit preprocessing-success inclusion criteria (Table with demographics, ADI-R/ADOS/IQ reported).
Custom SPM8 pipeline fully specified step-by-step (slice timing, realignment, coregistration, normalization, nuisance regression, motion scrubbing) with a 7266-ROI gray-matter lattice.
Diagnosis source given as the ABIDE phenotypic file with reported ADI-R, ADOS, and IQ instrument scores for subgroups.

Leave-one-out classifier with age/sex/handedness/site covariates is well described, but it is not stated whether connection selection (t-test-based binning) was recomputed excluding the left-out subject at every iteration or on a dataset including that subject.

risk_of_bias.summary: A methodologically transparent, large multisite ABIDE I replication attempt; the main appraisal uncertainty is whether per-connection statistical selection was leakage-free within the leave-one-out loop.

charting.title: Multisite functional connectivity MRI classification of autism: ABIDE results
charting.authors: Nielsen JA; Zielinski BA; Fletcher PT; Alexander AL; Lange N; Bigler ED; Lainhart JE; Anderson JS
charting.diagnosis_assessment: ADI-R, ADOS (reported for subset of subjects, per-site)
charting.specific_features: Pairwise functional connectivity across a 7266-ROI whole-brain gray-matter lattice (26.4 million connections)
charting.importance_method: Binning of connections by discriminative strength; per-site accuracy by connection bin
charting.top_features_identified: Default mode network, parahippocampal and fusiform gyri, insula, Wernicke area, intraparietal sulcus connections
charting.specific_algorithms: Leave-one-out classifier on binned connections, with age, age-squared, gender, handedness and site as covariates
charting.key_performance_results: Best whole-brain classification accuracy was 60%, above chance but lower than previously reported single-site accuracy of about 80%
charting.summary_key_findings: Replicating a single-site connectivity classifier approach on the full multisite ABIDE I sample (964 subjects, 16 sites) yields 60% leave-one-out classification accuracy, substantially lower than previously reported single-site accuracy (~80%), with the most discriminative connections involving the default mode network, parahippocampal/fusiform gyri, insula, Wernicke area and intraparietal sulcus.
charting.features_associated_disorder: Default mode network, parahippocampal/fusiform gyri, insula, Wernicke area, intraparietal sulcus connections most discriminative of autism vs. control
charting.future_directions_recommended: Longer BOLD imaging times, controlled acquisition strategies, multimodal feature integration, and improved classification methods

narrative_row.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction; ABIDE I; 964 subjects (447 autism, 517 typically developing) from 16 sites
narrative_row.methods: Custom SPM8 preprocessing pipeline; whole-brain functional connectivity over a 7266-ROI gray-matter lattice; leave-one-subject-out classifier with age, age-squared, gender, handedness and site as covariates
narrative_row.outcomes: Maximum 60% whole-brain classification accuracy, above chance but below the ~80% previously reported for single-site classification; most discriminative connections involved default mode network, parahippocampal/fusiform gyri, insula, Wernicke area, and intraparietal sulcus; classifier score correlated with symptom severity, social function, daily living skills and verbal IQ
narrative_row.key_limitations: Multisite heterogeneity substantially degrades classification accuracy relative to single-site results; accuracy was significantly higher for sites with longer BOLD scan durations
narrative_row.relevance_notes: An early, influential multisite ABIDE I benchmark showing that cross-site connectivity classification underperforms single-site classification, motivating later work on pipeline/atlas choice and site-aware cross-validation

kg_link.cohort_description: 964 of 1112 ABIDE I subjects (447 autism, 517 typically developing) from 16 sites meeting preprocessing-success inclusion criteria and a minimum of 20 subjects per site
kg_link.pipeline: Custom SPM8 pipeline (slice timing, realignment, coregistration, normalization, nuisance regression, motion scrubbing)
kg_link.atlas: 7266-ROI whole-brain gray-matter voxel lattice (no named cortical atlas)
kg_link.finding: Leave-one-out whole-brain connectivity classification achieved up to 60% accuracy distinguishing autism from typical development, with the most discriminative connections in the default mode network, parahippocampal/fusiform gyri, insula, Wernicke area and intraparietal sulcus.
evidence_quotes: A total of 964 subjects met all inclusion criteria (517 typically developing subjects and 447 subjects with autism from 16 sites).

As high as 60% accuracy was obtained for whole brain classiﬁcation, with the best accuracy from connections involving regions of the default mode network, parahippocampaland fusiform gyri, insula, Wernicke Area, and intraparietal sulcus.
